newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya tea output falls over 40 pct in Jan-April.
newsitem.headline: Kenya tea output falls over 40 pct in Jan-April.

text.p: Kenya's tea production fell some 41 percent in January to April 1997 compared with the same period last year, Africa Tea Brokers (ATB) said on Tuesday.

Output for April 1997 was 10.92 million kg, a fall of 12.57 million kg or 53.58 percent from April 1996 while the cumulative figure for January to April was 54.97 million kg, 38.47 million kg or 41.17 percent below January-April last year, the Mombasa-based traders said in a report.

They said rainfall had given way to longer periods of sunshine in key growing areas but temperatures remained low and growth was inhibited. Most areas had recovered from severe drought and leaf intake was about average for the period.

Four sales were held in April when a total of 123,242 packages were sold at an average price of $1.99 per kg. Comparative figures for the same month last year were 313,093 packages sold at an average price of $1.43.

ATB figures showed production in Malawi at 17.83 million kg in January to March compared with 16.88 million in the first quarter of last year. There were no March figures for Uganda but production in January-March was 3.8 million kg from 3.90 million in the same period in the previous year.

It gave the January-April total production in Tanzania at 2.42 million kg compared to 2.13 million kg in the comparative period in 1996. It showed production in Zimbabwe at 4.39 million kg in January-April compared to that period the previous year.
ATB posted output on the Indian Ocean island of Mauritius at 2.20 million kg in 1996 from 3.78 million kg in 1995. It provided no figures for any period in 1997.

ATB showed the average price of Kenyan tea as $2.03 per kg in the period January-April compared to $1.46 the previous year. Ugandan prices were $1.84 from $1.16, Rwanda's $1.94 from $1.23, Zaire's $1.45 from $0.88 and Tanzania's $1.85 from $1.17.

On the Kenyan crop, ATB said: "Most areas have recovered from the severe drought and factories have now reverted to normal production. However, current cold temperatures will to some extent inhibit growth."
It added on Malawi's crop "The weather pattern remains unchanged with a further decline in crops (expected)."

Seasonal short rains failed in Kenya in October to December last year. A dry spell persisted until seasonal long rains arrived late in March. Kenya's economic planningh ministry had already forecast a production fall this year on account of the drought but had not envisaged ATB's dramatic figures.
Kenya was ranked as the world's top exporter of black teas last year when its production was a record 257 million kg. Tea is Kenya's second main foreign exchange earner behind tourism.
